A Real-Time Strategy

Cosy Empires

You lead the Sunfolk against the Ashkin.
Difficulty: Medium

Build 16 August 2026

Choose your match
You have a saved village. Starting a new game will write over it at the next dawn.

You start with one villager and a town centre in ruins.

  • Tap your villager, then tap Gather and tap a tree — or double-tap them and after that every tap just does whatever makes sense where you tapped
  • Bring back wood until there is enough to repair the town centre
  • Then build it out, however you like, into a cosy empire

Something new happens every day. Get everyone indoors at night — there are things out in the dark. And each season brings its own.

Settings

Difficulty is set when you start a game, and can be changed at any time from the ☰ menu, top left — it starts a fresh map.

Sound and a few other things will live here once they exist.

Patch notes
Patch 21.17
Fixed
  • Continuing a saved village after actually closing and reopening the game (rather than just staying on the same page) could throw the moment anything with grass on it came into view, and every frame after it. A cache of baked grass images was being written into the save as a set of hollow shells that only look real once the browser has properly forgotten them — harmless in testing, but not in an actual saved game reopened later. Villages saved before this fix are repaired automatically the next time they load
  • The Captain's Station had no upgrade of its own, the one building that had slipped through when every other building was given one. It now has a Muster Ground rung, training the Captain a little faster
  • Wandering pilgrims could get wedged against a building or a shoreline and stay there for the rest of their visit. Their own "am I making progress" check was judged frame to frame, which a pilgrim nudged back and forth at a corner could pass on plenty of individual frames while going nowhere overall - the same blind spot villagers themselves had before they were given a check judged over a few seconds instead of one frame at a time. Pilgrims now use that same steadier check
  • Double-tapping the town icon to bring the camera home did nothing during the Wandering Age, right when a lone founder is most likely to need it - it was quietly requiring the town centre to be fully built, not just standing
A few small signs of life
  • A soldier fighting badly hurt now shows it in how they move — a slight limp, one arm held a little in — rather than only in a health bar
  • A villager with genuinely nothing on — not working, not walking anywhere, not sat down — sways gently now and again instead of standing dead still
  • A couple who spent the day together get one warm light at their own door as they turn in for the night
  • The Noticeboard occasionally reports on a couple out and about instead of the day's usual history fact
  • A sleeping villager's dream can now, about half the time, carry a soft hint of tomorrow's weather
  • A fighter right at death's door trembles a little rather than standing perfectly steady through the last of it
  • An earned name keeps meaning something afterwards — Stonehand mines a touch faster, Timberarm cuts a touch faster, and the same for the field-earned name at their own farm
  • A household that lived through a bad night stays wary of the woods for a while — still out and about, just not for an afternoon reading under a tree
  • A night event that hasn't turned up in a long while is now a little more likely to be the one that does, rather than a long game leaning on the same handful of common ones forever
  • The Noticeboard can now report on the village's own prosperity — a running read of population, buildings, named villagers and discoveries, not a target to hit, just something to feel good about
  • A new "Then…" order button: arm it and the next order given to a unit that's already busy is remembered rather than replacing what they're doing, and taken up the moment that job actually finishes — queue "build this, then gather" in two taps instead of waiting for the first to be done
  • The baker's whites no longer darken with the cold like everyone else's clothes — he's meant to be recognisable at a glance year-round, and winter was quietly working against that
  • The baker doesn't just stand at his own door on a quiet day — when there's no round to run he ducks inside for a spell, or carries a loaf over to somebody's house, so he's doing something even between rounds
  • The Caretaker's Cottage now banks up to three replenishes in one visit instead of one — a busy farm could run dry before he walked all the way back round to it again
  • A Granary now sends out its own farmhand, walking out to one of your farms and back — a sight, not a mechanic, so a farm reads as somewhere someone actually goes
  • The baker has a third thing to do on a quiet day now, besides ducking inside or visiting a house — pottering about right outside his own oven
  • A soldier who has come through enough fighting now carries a small permanent mark of it — a pale streak through their helm's crest, never a stat change, so an army isn't purely disposable identical bodies
  • A nightcap at the hearth: most nights now, a handful of villagers pause at the town centre for a few minutes before bed for one last wordless chat — a light, common cousin of the rare night the elder tells a story by the fire
  • Dusk no longer sends the whole village home on the exact same frame — everyone gets a few seconds of "just finishing up" first, staggered per villager, so the village winds down rather than snapping over like a light switch
  • Night fishing now has a moment worth reacting to — watch for the float jerking hard instead of its usual steady bob, and tap your angler quickly for a bonus catch on top of the ordinary moonlit haul. Miss it and it costs nothing
  • The Night Market is no longer a total ambush — if a cart is coming tonight, the almanac says so a day ahead, so trading with it (and the raid risk that comes with buying) is a decision you can actually plan for
  • Once you've met the hermit, autumn brings a small ask of your own — a little wood before winter, given by tapping a carrying villager onto the hermit itself. Miss the season and there's always next year
  • A storm passing, or rough weather clearing, can wash a shipwrecked chest up along the water's edge — a one-off find of gold and salvaged wood, worth a look before someone else's tide takes it back
  • A message in a bottle can wash up too, now and then — a mysterious note with a genuine playing tip rolled up inside. Leave it too long and it washes back out, but another can always turn up another night
  • A villager claims a house of their own well before dusk now, rather than having nowhere to call home until night sends them looking, and one with truly nothing to do will sometimes wander a few tiles on their own rather than standing dead still all day
  • Repairing one of the five ancient ruins is a real decision now, not a free find — once fully mended it waits for you to choose and pay for how to finish it: the safe, familiar way, or a costlier, more ambitious one with a bigger payoff
  • A repaired ruin now carries a small plaque set into its own wall — a quiet mark that this one is found, finished, and someone chose how
  • A new Iron Age building, the Sunstone Cairn: it produces nothing, trains nothing and defends nothing, and costs more than anything else you can build — a wonder for a village with nothing left to spend on, and nowhere to put it but pride
  • A rare night can now be a proper meteor shower too, not only a lantern festival — half the village comes out to watch, on top of the ordinary run of falling-star wishes
  • A thriving village now genuinely feels busier, not just older — how many off-duty villagers you'll ever see out and about at once grows with the village's own prosperity, not a flat number every village was stuck with regardless of size
  • A new Bronze Age order, Fortify: send a villager to a wall, tower or your fortress and pay a little wood and stone for a temporary shield — real extra protection that soaks up damage before your walls take it, and runs out on its own after a while if it's never needed
  • A new Village Chronicle on the start menu — a short memory of your last ten matches, win or lose: who founded it, how far it got, and how it ended. Separate from your one saved village, so nothing about it is ever at risk
  • The date at the bottom of the screen now traces the day itself — a thin ring behind it, with the sun riding the top half while it's up and the moon taking over the bottom half once it isn't, so you can see roughly how much of the day or night has gone at a glance
Patch 21.16
The Captain
  • A new hero-tier unit for the Iron Age: the Captain, trained at a new Captain's Station. Taller than anyone else in your army, bare-headed on purpose, carrying a kite shield and a blade that always carries a faint moonstone-blue light — a light-blue hue by day, a proper glow after dark, lighting the ground around him the way a torch would without carrying one
  • Only one can ever be in service at a time — training a second is refused, whether it would come from the same station or another one, until the first falls
  • His attack cycles through three distinct swings — from the left, from the right, then an overhead slam that throws whoever he's fighting off their feet. He plants his feet and trades blows rather than circling his target the way the rest of the army does
  • The Captain's Station itself is sized like the Caretaker's Cottage, built in ash-grey stone rather than the usual timber, with a pair of spare blades crossed by the door

Stats and training cost are still a placeholder — the finished unit is meant to cost a real share of every resource, moonstone included. The knock-people-into-the-air slam is in; a leadership buff for nearby soldiers is not built yet.

Patch 21.15
Fixed
  • Some Ashkin villages could get permanently stuck before ever reaching the Stone Age — a small enough economy meant nobody was ever put to gathering wood specifically, so the settlement sat on plenty of everything else and never quite the timber the next step needed. They now always keep enough hands free early on to actually get past it, whichever way they otherwise like to play
  • A small-economy Ashkin could field a real army on Peaceful but never build a single wall or tower, since that only used to kick in with a bigger village than that kind of side ever keeps. Now it doesn't take nearly as much
Patch 21.14
Floyd
  • Gumby has company — Floyd, a second little dog, smaller again and after something different: where Gumby raids a farm, Floyd makes off with a sock from the nearest house. Tap either one to see who they are
Peaceful keeps growing
  • The Ashkin on Peaceful now keep building the whole match through — more villagers, more soldiers, a wall or two, a watchtower, an armoury — instead of stalling out partway. They still never march on you first: leave them be and they simply become a steadily bigger, better-defended village, so the longer a match runs the more there eventually is to reckon with if you do pick the fight
Fixed
  • Gumby could spawn standing on ground he could not actually stand on, and would then never move again for the rest of the match — about one visit in four. He (and Floyd) now check the ground is clear before trotting in
  • On Peaceful, the Ashkin's army could sit stuck at the same size for a real stretch of the match while resources piled up waiting on the next age — and on some maps, holding every resource back at once meant they never quite banked enough food to age up at all, however much everything else piled up
Patch 21.13
Ground, sky, and the light between them
  • The wind travels now. It was one number that every blade, tree and field obeyed at the same instant. A gust is a band that crosses the country instead: the grass goes over in a ripple, the trees on the far side lean a beat later, the crops bend as it reaches them, and it passes on
  • Every bird goes up before the rain. A quarter of a minute before the first drop the roofs empty, a flock lifts out of the fields, and they are gone — the same warning the light gives, in the language birds use. Once per spell
  • Once a season, the air fills with something. The firefly swarm was the best small thing in the game and it only ever happened after dark — so now every season has its own, by day, and you will see it at least once in each: Bloomtide beetles in spring, every one a different pastel; dragonflies in summer that hang still and are then twenty feet away; gossamer on the wind in autumn; and diamond dust in winter, crystals of ice hanging in the cold and flashing in the sun. None of them does anything. That is the point of them
  • The sea has depth to it now — deeper water out from the shore and lighter shallows against it, swell running at two different scales, and torn scraps of foam at the edge instead of the row of perfect circles that used to sit there
  • Reeds at the water's edge, which lay over when a squall comes across the water. And at dusk and dawn a fish rises on still water and leaves a ring spreading behind it
  • Grass, everywhere the ground is grass. It leans on the same wind that moves everything else, and a few blades cross the boots of whoever is standing in it — they bend aside as somebody walks through and spring back behind them. Nothing is ever hidden in it
  • Lean in and there is more there. Close to, a finer bed appears that does not exist further out: taller wisps, and seed heads once you are right in. Pull back and the grass steps aside for the big picture
  • The water moves at every edge. A swell runs ALONG the coast rather than pulsing everywhere at once, foam breaks at the top of each run, and the wet sand it leaves behind lags a moment behind the water — which is what makes the sea look like it is going out rather than just shrinking. Rough weather runs it up harder
  • There are clouds now, not just their shadows. Pull out and you can see them crossing above the valley, with their shade crawling below and behind them — the gap between the two is the height. Come in close and they fade to almost nothing, as a cloud should when you are looking at somebody's boots
  • It goes grey before it rains. The light starts draining out of the day about half a minute before the first drop and keeps going until it breaks. The almanac tells you in words; this tells you in the language weather actually uses. And the ground is never quite the same shade twice
Day one
  • A new match now opens with three lines and an X: you have woken alone, gather wood to repair your town, stay safe at night and attack if you have to. The world waits until you close it. It also tells you the two ways back if you get lost — tap Idle to find your villager, double-tap the small town icon on the row of group numbers to get home. Loading a village you already have does not show it, you have read it
  • Your first villager carries a torch. They are the only villager who ever does. You begin with one person, on a map you have not walked, and a lone civilian carried no light at all — so the moment it got dark you lost sight of the only thing you had
  • Goblin camps get teeth from level two. A camp that has come back stronger fields archers and puts up lookouts — lashed poles with a hide platform, and they shoot. It also brings war brutes: half again the size of an ordinary goblin, that much harder to put down, with a ridge of a mohawk and a bone guard on the shoulder so you can see one coming. Their club comes round in an arc and catches whoever else is stood beside the one it swung at, so a line drawn up shoulder to shoulder in front of one is the wrong shape to fight it in
  • Their clubs are proper weapons now — dark wood against the skin rather than the same brown as the arm holding it, with small iron spikes set into the head. It is the only metal anywhere on a goblin, which is what makes the club look like something they made rather than a branch they found
  • The camp itself shows its level: a second rank of stakes, lashings in the tribe's own colour, and a rack of bones by the door from level three. None of it starts anything. You can walk right under a lookout and it will watch you go — and now you really can, because a sleeping camp used to kill anything that wandered within a few paces of it while insisting it had never noticed you
  • Villagers pick berries by hand. They had a felling axe out and were swinging it at the fruit — and at wheat fields, come to that. Now they reach into the bush, one hand in as the other comes out, turning to face whatever they are working. You can see a berry in the hand on the way back, and the basket they carry home holds the fruit in the colour it actually was when it was picked
  • The fruit ripens as the season runs. Each season walks its berries through three colours and the bushes shift between them, so a patch you gathered from at the start of autumn is a different colour by the end of it — green and hard, then blushing, then ripe in spring; scarlet, then damson, then sloe-dark in autumn. Every bush keeps its own clock, so the one in the sun ripens first
  • You hear the goblins before you see them. The first camp of a season announces itself in four steps as you close on it: chanting somewhere out in the dark at night, then voices arguing in a language of hard sounds, then a shout going up when they spot you, then war drums — and they still do not move. Walk away and the drums fall away behind you. By the time you have met them once, only the drums still play
  • The berry bushes are properly drawn now. They were one flat green ellipse with four red dots on it — and they are the first thing you ever walk up to. Now there are four different bushes, built in layers with a ragged leafy edge, and they turn with the year: rusty in autumn, in blossom with the fruit still green in spring, twigs under snow in winter. Five small matte berries when full, fewer as they are picked, so a bush that has been worked looks picked over rather than shrunk
  • Three berry bushes at your town, and only three. A start used to be ringed with twenty of them, which made the first half hour a walk between berries rather than a reason to build a farm. Three is about three hundred food: a second and third pair of hands, and a field to put them on. Wild berries out in the country are half as common as they were — worth sending a scout for, not enough to live on
Mist, and a foggy day
  • Mist now gathers in the low ground. It lies between the ground and the village — roofs, people and lamplight stand clear above it, and what it does is mute the ground it is lying on. It is thickest by the water, thin on open ground, and after dark you mostly see it where there is light to see it by
  • You will catch it at dusk, through the night, and at dawn, where it is heaviest. It comes up on its own and burns off slowly when the sun gets to it rather than blinking out. Nothing about it is still: every bank sways, rolls and swells on its own slow clock
  • “A foggy day” is now real weather, and the almanac will forecast it. A season that rolls weather may roll fog instead of its own rough spell — autumn is the foggy season, spring nearly as much, a summer fog is rare
  • It is the one weather that is not rough. Nothing is damaged, no brazier is blown out, and you can walk in it perfectly well. What a fog takes is your sight: you cannot see as far in it as in anything else, a blizzard included. The birds stay out too — it is only hazy, not foul
Something passing the camera
  • Once in a while something crosses right in front of you at night, far too big to be standing on the map — a moth in the warm half of the year, a bat in the cold. It is past in a second and a half. It did not fly across the village; it flew past you
  • By day, seeds, blossom, leaves or frost blow between you and the village, close to the lens and out of focus. They slide faster than the ground does when you move the camera, which is what makes them look near
  • Both are treats rather than furniture — about one match in four, like a sky full of stars
And a sky that stayed one evening
  • A starry sky now belongs to the night it turned up in. It used to hang over the morning if the night ended first, and weather could close in over the top of it. Either one puts it out now, easing away over a few seconds rather than vanishing between two frames
Patch 21.12
Villagers you actually know
  • A villager can earn a name. Most of your village never will — and that is the point. The handful who have one have it because of something they did, and the panel will tell you what
  • Four ways to earn it. Stand through the first night and live. Sit through three of the elder's stories. Work one job for a whole season without being shuffled off it. Or be picked out by the world itself — led away by a fox, sat at the hermit's fire, carrying a season's seed home
  • The name fits the deed: Bjorn Frostwake for standing through a winter night, Arne Timberarm for a season at the trees, Runa Foxfriend, Ylva the Well-Told. Your founder is the First
  • You are told the moment somebody earns one — an anonymous villager becoming a person in front of you is the whole point of it. The first deed is the one that names them; anything later is kept in their record but never renames somebody you already know
  • Tap one and the panel says who they are, how long they have been about and what they have done. And if somebody you know by name is killed, you are told which one
A world without dead ground
  • Map generation used to leave threads of land one tile wide winding through the water where a pond had cut through a coast. Nothing can be built on them — not even the smallest building — so they were dead ground that looked like somewhere you could settle. They are gone: any land that is not part of a solid two-by-two is taken back by the water, and the new shoreline gets its sand like any other
Goblins — Peaceful gets something to fight
  • Peaceful has an enemy now, and it is entirely up to you whether you ever meet it. Somewhere out in the unexplored country a goblin camp is pitched: a hide hut, a couple of shacks and five goblins hanging about. They will never come for you. You have to go and find them, and then you have to start it
  • Start it and you have started it properly. Hit one goblin, or one of their buildings, and the war drums go up and the whole camp comes for you until it is levelled. Everything of theirs has to go — every goblin and the hut — and clearing it pays 100 of every resource, carried home
  • They are tied to the seasons. A camp belongs to the season it turns up in, and there are four tribes: the same goblins, in four different skins and four different warpaints. Spring is sour green with a stripe up the face, summer tan with a red band across the eyes, autumn russet with claw-slashes, winter grey-blue with rings round the eyes like sockets
  • Beat one and next year that season comes back a level harder, up to level five. Levels show as an added colour on their belts, wrists and clubs — blue, black, silver, then gold — so a level four autumn goblin is plainly the same autumn tribe in better kit. Leave a camp alone and it strikes its tents when the season turns and comes back next year exactly as it was, so nothing is ever lost by walking away
  • The camp pitches somewhere new every year, always well away from both villages and always out in ground you have not walked. Torches burn either side of their hut and light the camp as far as your own hall lights yours — but a camp you have not found yet stays dark, so it never gives its own position away
  • The Ashkin have no quarrel with them and they have none with the Ashkin. This is your war, and only if you want one
  • Your Noticeboard keeps the tally — four seasons, five pips each, filled in as far as you have got, and what level is waiting for you next
The first night, and the one who started it all
  • Your very first villager has a name now, from the moment the match begins, and the panel says so: their name, and underneath it, that they founded your village. Months into a Peaceful village you can still tap them and see who the whole place grew out of. There are 168 names to draw on — Norse, Old English and Swedish — so you are not running a town of nine people all called Bjorn
  • The first night now comes for you every single time, not two starts in three, and what comes depends on the season you began in: a bramble beast in spring, a dust scorpion in summer, a night bear in autumn putting on weight before the cold, and the frost lynx in winter
  • And it will not fight itself. Your villager used to turn and defend themselves without being asked; they do not any more. Select them and send them at it, or they die — and with the town centre still a ruin, that is your run. You get a clear warning when it appears and one more nudge if you have not moved. It is the first thing the game actually asks you to do
  • Send them at it and they will win, but it is a real fight, not a formality — expect to come out of it at about a quarter health. Rest puts it right: they mend steadily once nothing is biting them, so surviving the night is not a wound you carry for the rest of the match
  • On Peaceful it can never take more than two thirds of them. The lesson still lands — something comes out of the dark, they are mauled, and it is plainly your job to do something about it — but a Peaceful village is never lost to it. Every other difficulty means it
The small hours
  • The night is not just a darker version of the day any more. There are small things about: moths that gather at your braziers, the odd drifting firefly, and spiders hanging on threads by the walls
  • Which of them are out depends on the season — moths and fireflies from spring, spiders arriving with the autumn. Winter is nearly empty, because nearly nothing flies in winter: a few spiders sheltering by the buildings and that is all. The quiet is the point
  • And rarely — about one night in six — a single glow bug, crawling low with a steady light of its own. It is meant to be a thing you notice and point at rather than scenery, so there is never a field of them. Each season has its own colour: new green in spring, warm gold through summer, an ember orange in autumn, and a cold pale blue in the snow — the only light out there on a winter night
  • They are gone by morning, the way they are gone when you go looking in the daylight. Every one of them has its own size, its own speed and its own wander, and there is a breeze that moves the lot of them together
  • The firefly swarm is untouched and still its own rare, announced occasion. This is the everyday texture underneath it
The baker's round
  • Somebody works at the Bakery now. During the day he comes out in his whites and his tall hat, with a basket of loaves in both arms, and walks to wherever your soldiers actually are — a barracks, a range, or a company camped out in the open. Bread handed round, empty basket, back to the oven. He does not go out after dark
  • He works out where the round is worth walking, rather than simply going to the nearest thing: he counts how many hungry soldiers each stop would actually reach and goes where the army is. Villagers get nothing — it is the soldiers' bread — and neither does the scout out exploring, or he would spend all day walking to one man
  • A loaf lasts a day. The Bakery's own bonus and its upgrades are still the full-time part and have not changed; this is on top, and it wears off by tomorrow morning. So there is a right moment to attack — catch your army just after the bread has gone round and they hit harder than they will in the morning
  • He is one of the same people as everyone else out there, drawn the same way, with his own face and height under the coat. He costs no population, cannot be selected or ordered, and nothing can hurt him
The old smith's own way
  • Repairing the Old Blacksmith used to hand you its ancient tempering free, the moment the last stone went in. It is the fourth and best level of armour in the game, so you buy it now — at that forge, and at no other forge anywhere. What finding the ruin gets you is the only place in the world that sells it
  • One purchase, all three armour lines at once, and it stacks on top of whatever ordinary tier each of them has separately reached. It wants the Iron Age and 140 iron and 120 gold — dearer than tier two, as the level above it should be
  • Before the Iron Age the forge names it and shows it greyed rather than hiding it. You went and found the thing; you should be able to see what it is for
The caretaker gets up and goes
  • The Caretaker's Cottage used to top up your farms by changing a number where nobody could see it. Now somebody actually lives there. They come out of the door, walk across the village to whichever field is lowest, spend a while sowing it, and walk home again
  • They look and move like everybody else out there, because they are drawn as one of them — their own face, their own height, their own clothes. They cost no population, cannot be selected or ordered, and nothing can hurt them. They are simply somebody doing a job
  • The wood is paid when they arrive, not when they set off. Spend your last log while they are still walking and they turn round and come home rather than sowing a field out of nothing. Knock the cottage down and its caretaker goes with it; build two and there are two of them
Every building can be improved
  • Every single building in the game now has an upgrade in every age it is able to stand in. Select one and its own next improvement is there in the panel, named, priced and with a line saying what it does. A farm, lumber camp, mine or house can be improved four times — the first of them while you are still a camp, before the Stone Age has been paid for. A Stone Age building has three, a Bronze Age one two, and an Iron Age building has its single one
  • They belong to the building, not to you. Four barracks are four separate ladders and four separate bills — the same way the gather research and the watchtower rebuild have always worked. And the work mends what it touches, so a damaged building comes out of an upgrade whole
  • Each one does something you can feel rather than a number going up: a Drill Yard turns recruits out faster, a Second Hearth makes room for another family, a Timber Chute sends the logs down to the camp on their own, Standing Stones give the village something to think about, Iron Battlements give a fortress the reach to use them. Nothing is filler
  • Several buildings that quietly did nothing at all now do something. The Shrine and the Noticeboard produce knowledge once they have been built up. The Trading Post finally earns its keep — your own scales, and a better rate on every trade you make. The Well waters a village that works better for it
  • The four that already had a research line — farm, lumber camp, mine and the Elder's Lodge — kept it, and gained the rungs below it. So does the brazier. Only ever one upgrade is offered at a time, so what you see is a single ladder that carries on all the way up rather than two competing buttons
  • The Ashkin buy them too, one at a time, and hold back what they owe on their own town centre before they spend on anything else
  • None of it is lost on an old village: anything saved before this simply starts at the bottom of its ladder with everything still to climb
The camp, and then the village
  • Getting the town centre standing no longer hands you the whole game at once. It makes you a camp: there is a bed, the hearth is lit, the wilds start taking an interest — and you may build a farm, a lumber camp, a mine and houses. That is what a camp does. Everything else waits
  • What ends the Wandering Age is upgrading the town centre, on the same button every other age-up has always used: 100 wood and 50 food, and your people enter the Stone Age with the rest of the build order open to them. Measured over a dozen matches, the camp lasts about three days — long enough to be a stage of the game rather than a loading screen
  • The almanac says Wandering Age for the whole of it, camp and all, and only turns over to Stone Age when you have actually paid for it
  • The Ashkin live under exactly the same rule, hold back exactly the same hundred wood, and cannot start on a barracks before you can
  • Villages already in progress are not sent back for any of this. Anything with a town centre standing is in the Stone Age on load and is not charged for it a second time — whether it was saved last week or an hour ago
Before the Stone Age
  • A match no longer opens with a working town and five pairs of hands. It opens in the Wandering Age: one villager, nothing whatever in the stores, and the town centre standing in ruins. There is no build menu and nobody to train — the only job in the world is to fetch the 70 wood the repair wants, and do it. Roughly a day's work
  • Wherever you start, the ground provides: berries within a few paces of the ruin — enough for a second pair of hands and a farm besides — and trees close enough to begin on straight away. Whether the opening is work or a search should not come down to the roll of a map
  • And while you are still out there, your people see further than they will once they are settled. One villager and no scout is little enough without searching blind as well
  • Get it standing and your people settle: the roof goes on, the hearth is lit, and the Stone Age begins. Only then do you find out what this particular ground was good for — the village's own small gift is held back until there is a village to give it to
  • Until the centre stands there is nowhere to sleep, and a night in the open tells. Anyone who spends it out there is dead on their feet by morning and works and walks at a fraction of their pace — nobody dies of it, but you will feel it. One night indoors puts it right, and once you are settled it stops being a worry at all
  • The Ashkin start exactly the same way and have to do the same work, so it is a race out of the rubble rather than a handicap. On a harder difficulty their ruin is further along than yours to begin with
  • Nothing in the dark will come for you while you are still in the ruins. With one pair of hands and no walls, a single hungry animal on the second night would not maim somebody — it would end the game outright, with nothing you could have done. The wilds notice you the moment the hearth is lit, and from then on the night is exactly as dangerous as it always was
  • Your first night is not always a quiet one. Two times in three something comes out of the dark for whoever is out there — a lynx in winter, a wolf otherwise. They will turn and fight it without being told to, they will come off much the worse for it, and it will break off and slink away rather than finish them. They mend by morning. The dark has things in it, and you want a roof: that is the whole lesson, and it costs you nothing but a fright
  • And if you are ever left with a standing town centre and nobody at all to work it, somebody wanders in out of the trees after a while and takes up the work. Only ever down to nought, and never as an income
Carrying it home
  • What a villager is carrying used to be a small coloured square floating by their head from the first swing of the axe. Now you see nothing until they turn for home — and then it is in both arms: logs with the cut ends showing, blocks of stone, ingots of gold or iron, a basket of berries, or moonstone that gives off its own light
  • The axe goes away for the walk. You cannot carry an armful of logs and swing a felling axe at the same time
  • And a miner swings a pickaxe now, rather than the same axe the berry-pickers carry
Dressed for the work
  • You can tell what somebody does by looking at them now. Anyone out in the fields is in a broad straw hat, anyone at the trees is in a woodcutter's check flannel, and anyone up at the stone, gold, iron or moonstone wears a hard hat with a lamp on the front — and once it is dark, that lamp is lit
  • It follows the work and not the villager, so somebody sent from the woods up to the quarry has changed by the time they get there
Things to do
  • Seven more ways for somebody off duty to spend an afternoon, on top of watching the farm, skipping stones, reading under a tree and flying a kite. One will sit down outside the town centre and play a guitar. Another will stand and sing — and the singing spreads: whoever is near enough to hear stops what they are doing and goes off humming it themselves, so a whole corner of the village ends up at it. Someone else will stand about working a yo-yo. And someone will pick a bunch of flowers and go and give them to whoever is nearest
  • Three of them belong to a season and only turn up in it. A snowball is winter — and whoever gets hit packs one and throws it straight back. A running jump into a pile of leaves is autumn, leaves and all. And a puddle the rain left behind is there to be jumped in, as anybody stood too close finds out
  • The whole batch is people doing things to each other rather than beside each other. There are rather more of them out and about, too: with a dozen things to do and half of them seasonal, the old rate meant you could watch a whole afternoon and see two
Patch 21.11
Auto mode
  • Double-tap a villager to put just that one into Auto mode — the panel below says so. From then on, every tap does whatever actually makes sense there: attack an enemy, gather a resource, repair or join a build, garrison a watchtower as its lookout, or board a boat, all without arming an action button first
  • Tap bare ground to finish: Auto mode ends and the villager is let go, so you are left with nothing selected and can get straight on with something else. Before, there was no way out of it except tapping the villager themselves, which nobody found — and a tap on open ground just walked them over there instead. Tapping the villager still drops out of Auto mode as well, and it lets go on its own if they stop being your only selection, or if they die
Build menu
  • Build now opens onto five categories — Military, Food & Wood, Gold & Stone, Knowledge, Village — instead of one long sideways scroll through everything at once. Military leads with whatever actually trains a unit before the walls, towers and upgrades that don't
  • The rare one-villager unlocks (a seasonal crop, the Wildlings' Den, the Hermit's Cottage) still show the moment you open Build, above the categories, so they're never missed
Seasonal realism
  • A puddle now actually means something to walk through, not just a passing decal — ground still wet from a downpour or squall slows anyone crossing it, easing off as the puddle itself dries up
  • Sunflowers turn up here and there once summer's properly in, growing tall out of the ordinary wildflower patches rather than a whole field of them appearing at once
Groups
  • Group 1 is always the Town Centre now, not a spare numbered slot — tap it to select it, tap it twice to bring the camera straight home
Village life
  • The off-duty villagers who come out of the houses — the ones who watch the farm, skip stones, read under a tree or fly a kite — are drawn as the very same people as the villagers working around them: the same build, the same height, the same walk. They had a smaller, plainer figure all of their own before, which is why they never quite looked like they belonged. Only their clothes set them apart now, which was always the idea. They dress for the winter along with everybody else, too, and they have finally put the woodcutting axe down — one of them was flying a kite with it still in his fist
  • They no longer keep to their own doorstep. Somebody off duty will now walk right across the village to call in somewhere else — the bakery, the barracks, the town centre — and they find their way round whatever is in between rather than stopping against it
  • And one errand is no longer the whole afternoon: about half the time they will go on somewhere else before heading home, up to a couple more stops
  • They stop and talk, as well. Somebody on their way past an idle or gathering villager may pull up for a word — both of them stand and face each other for a few seconds, then get on with it. Two off-duty villagers who meet on the path will do the same, and someone will happily walk up to whoever is sat reading under a tree and interrupt them
  • And your own working villagers now do it themselves. Two of them at the same patch of woods will occasionally down tools for a few seconds, have a word, and get straight back to it — they never leave the job you gave them, never lose their order, and never do it while there is fighting in the village
Weather
  • A thunderstorm's rain no longer falls as one ruled sheet of identical streaks — every drop has its own weight, length, angle and speed now, the nearer ones heavier and brighter, and the whole downpour leans and slides as the gust comes and goes
Fixed
  • Moonstone Villagers could be trained and then had nothing they could actually do — gathering, building, and joining a building's crew were every one of them gated on being an ordinary villager, which they are not. The night shift works now: it gathers, it builds, it repairs, and it fights
  • The wandering pilgrims used to walk into the water and shuffle about in the shallows for the rest of their visit. They walk on out of sight instead
  • The moonlit hare and stag could end up standing inside a building, sliding through it or wedged against a wall until their next whim took them. They keep out of the walls now, and if a step would put them in one they think better of it and go somewhere else
  • An ancient ruin also punched a hole straight through the black fog when it appeared — it is placed as one of your own buildings so that repairing it works like any other repair, and that quietly gave it a building's eyesight. It lights nothing now until you have actually found it
  • Birds no longer fly over ground nobody has ever set foot on. A skein crossing the black told you there was something out there to see, which is the one thing unexplored fog is for
  • An ancient ruin used to announce itself the moment it appeared, while it was still sitting out in unexplored country. You had to be told about it rather than find it, which rather defeated the point. Nothing is said now until your own people have actually been out there and uncovered it — and once found, it stays found, without introducing itself again every time somebody wanders back past
  • A saved village from before the ancient ruins landed could fail to continue at all. Loading now fills in anything a save is missing from an earlier version, rather than losing the village over it
Patch 21.10
Things to find
  • Five ruins may now turn up somewhere near your village, rarely, one at a time — an old farmhouse, a blacksmith's, a shrine, a watchtower, and a mine. Each is hidden until you actually explore over it, broken, blackened and overgrown until you send villagers to repair it
  • Restored, each one turns out to have been worth finding: a better field than a fresh farm's, a watchtower that sees twice as far, a richer mine, a straight gift of moonstone, and a blacksmith whose own old trick tempers every soldier's armour a little further, at any age — look for a faint violet gleam on their shoulders
  • None of the five vanish once repaired, either — they keep a little of that broken, overgrown look for good, just less of it
Patch 21.9
A fuller night
  • Fishing after dark now pays off properly — a shoal bites better once it's truly deep night, at the Dock or from the bank
  • A falling star can still be wished on, but catch a few in quick succession during a meteor shower and each one sweetens the last
  • A rare, occasional night now brings something out of the ordinary — the first being a lantern festival, every house lit together and the village out and about, with a small reward for everyone while it lasts
  • Rarer still: a night market may set up at the edge of the village, offering better trades than the Trading Post can. Worth it, if you don't mind that buying more raises the odds of trouble before the cart moves on
New building
  • The Noticeboard now doubles as a logbook — open it to see which of the village's rarer sights you've actually come across this match
Patch 21.8
Put right
  • A creature wandering the village at night could walk up to a building and simply stop there, pinned against it for a few seconds, rather than finding its way round. Fixed for all of them — the dog, the wolf, the hare, the stag, and the fox
  • The fox was meant to dart playfully about the village while it lasted, but never actually moved from the spot it appeared in. It does now
Patch 21.7
Things to find
  • Two more moonlit visitors may pass through the village at night, alongside the wolf — each one worth three taps, moonstone every time. Still rare; that's the whole idea
Patch 21.6
New buildings
  • The Bakery — no gathering, no garrison, just an army that fights a little harder once it's standing
  • The Granary — your stores stop going off overnight
  • The Well and the Shrine — small and cheap, and not everything about them is built yet
  • The Blacksmith — every queue you have finishes a little faster while it stands
  • The Observatory — its lantern lights on its own when there's wild moonstone near your village tonight, even before you've found it
  • The Noticeboard — a true fact about the age you're living through, a new one each day
Patch 21.5
Things to find
  • Two more things worth noticing if you come across them — one in the weather, one in a light seen at the edge of the village at night. As before, no more said than that
  • Repairing the ancient ruin also gives every watchtower you hold a look to match — feathers and ivy, not just the extra reach
Put right
  • A creature that leads you somewhere could, rarely, end up leading nowhere at all — stuck across a stretch of water it had no way round. That's fixed, wherever it might have happened
Patch 21.4
Things to find
  • There are three things out in the world now worth noticing if you see them — a flower, a bird, a fox. Each leads somewhere, and each unlocks something new if you follow it through. Deliberately saying no more than that
  • Once a season, at night, a moonstone-coloured wolf may wander into the village. It doesn't mind being tapped — up to three times, and it's worth its while each time
Put right
  • Moonstone veins light the ground properly now — a real pool punched out of the dark, the same way a brazier's does, rather than a faint halo that was never bright enough to actually find one by
  • A watchtower's garrison — its archers and any villager keeping watch — can be released one at a time by tapping their face, the same as a barracks or range already worked
Patch 21.3
New building
  • The Caretaker's Cottage, in the Iron Age. It keeps your fields reseeded for you — no more hunting down a bare farm and tapping Replenish yourself
The night watch
  • A villager can be posted in a watchtower as a lookout, in a slot of their own alongside its four archers — the tower's panel now shows both counts separately
  • Spot moonstone from up there and they head straight out for it
  • Villagers get a Garrison button in place of Stop, since that's rather more useful to have to hand
Getting resources home
  • The Lumber Camp, Mine, Town Centre and Moonstone Manor each take deliveries at two points now, front and back. Boxed in on one side, a carrier finds the other instead of waiting on a wall that has no door
Put right
  • The cat known as Dog no longer walks on water
  • A villager worked a second night running with no rest used to drop dead without warning. There is a real stretch of time now where it shows on them and sending them home in time saves them
  • The Ashkin's villagers no longer sense — or wander into your town to mine — your Moonstone Manor's own vein
  • The fix that stopped the elder and the pilgrims leaning on a house forever only caught it once they were nearly there. A target properly walled in behind several buildings now gives up too, rather than pacing the outside of it for the rest of the match
Patch 21.2
Clearing ground
  • Villagers and moonstone villagers have a Remove button. Tap it, then tap a tree or a berry bush and it is gone on the spot — useful when the plot you want to build on has something standing in it
  • Nothing is carried home for it. It is not a harvest, it is getting the thing out of the way
  • It stays switched on so you can clear several in a row. It will not take a farm's crop, a shoal, stone, gold or moonstone, nor a tree your lumber camp was built to work
The town centre
  • It has a chimney at last — the tallest building in the village had a cold hearth while every cottage around it smoked. It draws harder while somebody is being trained inside
  • What has just been carried in is stacked by the door until it is put away
  • Its windows keep the hours now instead of blazing away at noon, and there is a lantern lit by the door after dark
  • The year leaves something on the step — blooms in spring, a leaning sheaf in autumn, snow shovelled aside in winter
  • A few chickens peck about in front of it by day, and go to roost after dark
Overhead
  • Some clear nights the sky will not keep still — one streak after another, for a minute or two, and then it settles
  • On a full moon, and only then, someone walks through by moonlight with the ground going pale where they pass. Notice them and they leave something behind
Out in the country
  • Rabbits have burrows. They graze within sight of one and bolt down it when anyone comes near, and put their heads out again a while later
  • Where there has been fighting, crows come by afterwards and wheel over the place for a time
  • Locusts can come down on a night's fields and strip a share of what is standing. A bad night, not a ruined harvest
  • Moonstone is twice as common at night. It was never as scarce as it looked — it is only ever out between dusk and dawn, and nobody is awake to notice
Put right
  • Peaceful means peaceful. The Ashkin will not march on you at all — not after twenty-five minutes, not ever — unless you go for them first. Defending your own ground does not count; going to their side of the valley does, and you will be told the day it happens
  • The Manor's own vein comes back. Mined flat, it had been gone for the rest of the match; it now fills again over two or three nights
  • Moonstone stops being minable at dawn, as it always should have — anyone still working a vein when the sun came up carried on all day
  • Moonstone glows harder after dark, and comes up earlier in the evening, so a vein is easier to come across — brighter again since, and there is a third more of it in your own veins each night. The Ashkin's are as they were
  • The elder and the pilgrims no longer lean on the side of a house for ever when the way round is blocked
  • The seasonal crop can no longer grow inside a tree, where it could not be picked
  • Butterflies keep off the trunks
  • Moonstone no longer comes up under a tree. Near enough half of every night's veins were sharing their ground with one, and a third of them were hidden behind it entirely — which was rather more to blame for veins being hard to find than the dark was. Veins now look for open ground, and on a night when there is none to be had they push the tree aside
  • Musicians can be told to follow your soldiers, which is rather the point of them — the order was offered and then refused
People and time
  • The days and nights are a fifth longer. More time in each, fewer of them in a match
  • The folk who step outside their houses look like the rest of the village now — hair, beards, scarves, hats, and no two quite the same height
  • The mark villagers were muttering that looked like a letter L has gone. Their chatter is meant to be wordless
  • One night event is away while it is rethought — the one that ringed a stray soldier with figures
Patch 21.1
  • Your village keeps itself now. It saves at every dawn, and the ☰ menu has a Save of its own for putting it down mid-afternoon
  • Continue on the start menu picks it back up — the same morning, the same people, the same ground you had walked
  • There is one village at a time. Starting a new game says so before it takes the old one
  • The start screen is a menu: new game, continue, how to play, settings, and these notes
  • Choosing a difficulty deals the match and shows you how to play before it starts — nothing moves until you say Begin
  • Settings can delete a saved village. There will be more in there before long
  • The island deals are away for the moment while the boats are finished
And out of the window
  • Flocks lean with the wind now — the same wind the chimney smoke and the grass have always leaned with
  • When the weather really gets up, the sky empties. Birds make for the nearest edge, the gulls stop coming, and the ridges clear until it eases
  • Twice a year a long skein crosses the whole map — away south as the leaves turn, back again in spring
  • The day has a round to it. Small things keep to the half-light at either end, deer come out into the open in the afternoon, and the big ones move at night
  • Something dry and brittle blows through on a windy summer or autumn afternoon
  • Frogs sit at the water's edge and hop, mostly nowhere. Walk up to one and it is gone
  • Every so often somebody's sheep gets out and ambles across your valley
  • The rain in a downpour falls a little slower, so it reads as rain rather than static
Patch 20.9
  • Moonstone is worth going out for now — the veins are richer, and they glow through ground you have already explored
  • Spend enough of it and you can raise something new in the Bronze Age. By day it works crystal; after dark it is a different building entirely
  • It comes with a vein of its own that never quite runs dry
  • There are people who keep the opposite hours to your village. They light the ground they walk on
  • They throw moonstone at anything that comes for your town, and whatever it hits does not shrug it off
  • Daylight does not suit them. You can work them through it, but not for ever
  • Give them somewhere of their own to live and there will be more of them — and little ones out after dark
  • Villagers can finally be put in a numbered group, with a tool of their own on the button
  • A night in their own bed mends anyone a little — whichever hours they keep
  • Longer messages now stay up long enough to actually be read
  • Fewer folk drifting out of doors, and the whales move on after a day or two
  • Moonstone comes up in three separate places around your village, and not every night — a night it does is worth staying up for
  • Fixed: dogs and children wandering out into the water
  • Fixed: the bottom row of buttons sitting too close to the edge on an iPad
  • Buildings can be worked through with crystal, once you have somewhere to work it — faster at whatever they do, and a light of their own after dark
  • Every kind of building takes the crystal differently: a seam through a field, a spine up a watchtower, a crown on the round roofs, spikes along a barracks
  • After dark a worked building is traced by the faintest blue line, and the crystal breathes very slowly — you will only catch it if you stop and watch one
  • The Ashkin get all of this too, if they ever get round to it. Moonstone is an indulgence, not their first thought
Patch 20.8
  • Something worth finding grows out in the deep country once a season. Bring it home and plant it
  • A new farm that does more than feed you
  • More moonstone after dark, and something that will show you the way
  • A full moon is worth more than a new one
  • Fireflies on warm nights, and two new sights in the sky
  • The rare sights are tuned to turn up about one match in five — so no single game shows you everything, and there is always something you have not seen yet
Patch 20.7
  • Braziers can be rebuilt once an age, each one on its own
  • Every rebuild throws its light further and stands up to more
  • And looks the part
Patch 20.6
  • The village settles in for the night gradually, house by house
  • Birds on your roofs, wind through the grass and smoke, and the odd shooting star
  • Buildings show their age. So do the people living in them
  • An almanac line at the bottom of the screen tells you about today
Patch 20.5
  • Twenty animals that only live well outside the town — five for each season
  • Squirrels, ducks, dragonflies, and a fox that never quite catches anything
  • Villagers take days off. Tap one to see who they are
  • Children, dogs, weather underfoot, and footprints in fresh snow
  • More happens at night
  • The Ashkin can cross to your island properly and attack together
